analysis.one_liner: Toughens mine safety enforcement, raises penalties for violators, and protects miners who report hazards.
analysis.headline: The mine safety bill never got a hearing or vote; it sat in a House subcommittee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill, named for the late Senator Robert C. Byrd and written in the aftermath of the 2010 Upper Big Branch explosion that killed 29 miners, would have rewritten federal mine safety law. It would have required independent investigations of deadly mine accidents, let federal investigators subpoena witnesses and interview miners privately, put mines with repeated safety violations under tighter watch, raised fines and created criminal liability for executives, and barred companies from firing miners who refuse dangerous work. The House committee it was sent to never took it up.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal miners and their families gain stronger protections: the right to speak to investigators without their boss present, full pay for up to 60 days when a mine is shut down for safety violations, protection from being fired for refusing unsafe work, and more training on their rights. Communities near mines benefit from independent investigations and stricter oversight of repeat violators.

how_it_helps.text: Requires an independent investigation panel, chaired by a federal safety research institute, for any mine accident involving three or more deaths, and requires investigators to determine why accidents happened and refer possible crimes to the Attorney General [S2]
Lets federal investigators question any miner privately, without the mine operator or its attorneys present, and gives the Labor Secretary subpoena power over witnesses and documents [S2]

Bars miners from being fired for refusing work they reasonably believe is a safety hazard, doubles the pay period they get when a mine is shut down for violations to up to 60 days, and adds criminal penalties for retaliation against miners who report hazards [S2]

Puts mines with recurring citations, accidents, or injuries into a 'pattern' status that brings more inspections, stricter benchmarks, higher fines, and lets the Labor Secretary collect fees from those operators for the extra inspections [S2]

Makes company officers and directors personally liable, civilly and criminally, for knowingly ordering or carrying out safety violations, and raises criminal penalties to up to $1 million and 5 years in prison for repeat violations that risk miners' lives [S3]

Requires mines to brief miners on hazards before each shift, tightens coal dust and rock dust standards to reduce explosion risk, requires atmospheric monitoring systems, and adds an hour of training on miners' legal rights to annual refresher training [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Coal mine operators bear the cost: higher fines, doubled penalties while in pattern status, fees for extra inspections, personal legal liability for executives, new monitoring and dust-control equipment, and up to 60 days of full pay for miners idled by safety shutdowns. Taxpayers fund the new independent investigation panels and hotline, though pattern-status mines reimburse inspection costs.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall hardest on smaller operators: new atmospheric monitoring systems, direct-reading dust monitors, added training hours, and up to 60 days of pay for idled miners are real expenses that could squeeze marginal mines [S2]

The bill lets the Labor Secretary shut down an entire mine on its own judgment of a 'continuing hazard' and makes it hard to challenge that decision in court, concentrating significant power in one agency [S3]
The tighter pattern-of-violations regime and employment protections could push marginal mines toward closure, which helps safety but can cost jobs in mining towns [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are life-and-death for the roughly tens of thousands of Americans who work underground: fewer explosions, dust disease, and retaliation cases. The costs are real but targeted — they fall on operators, heaviest on the repeat violators the bill is aimed at. A fair reading is that the bill trades meaningful compliance expense and expanded federal power for stronger protection of workers' lives.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in April 2011, sent to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, forwarded to its Workforce Protections subcommittee a month later, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2013 [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. George Miller introduced the bill on April 15, 2011, with 18 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support on record [S1] [S4]
The House referred it to the Committee on Education and the Workforce the day it was introduced [S5]
On May 20, 2011, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, and the record shows no further action for the rest of the 112th Congress [S5]
The bill never reached the House floor, and the Senate never considered a companion measure in the provided record [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal mine operators came out ahead: they avoided higher fines, personal liability for executives, fees for extra inspections, and a stricter pattern-of-violations regime for another two years. Miners got no new protections.

for.name: Rep. George Miller
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-CA), senior Democrat on the Education and Workforce Committee; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Robert C. Byrd Mine Safety Protection Act and led its promotion

for.name: 18 of 18 cosponsoring House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsored it

against.name: Rep. John Kline
against.role: Chairman, House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it to die in the Workforce Protections subcommittee

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, Republican-controlled in the 112th Congress
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after referring it to a subcommittee on May 20, 2011 [S5]

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 18 cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill sat in a committee run by Republicans, who took no action on it for the rest of the Congress.

industries.industry: Coal mining companies and their executives
industries.note: The bill raises fines, doubles penalties for repeat violators, collects fees for extra inspections, imposes new equipment and training costs, and makes officers and directors personally liable for knowingly violating safety law. Those costs are the flip side of protections miners would have gained.

industries.industry: Mine monitoring and safety equipment makers
industries.note: Mandates for atmospheric monitoring systems and direct-reading dust monitors would have created a market for that equipment. Safer mines are the point of the mandate.
